name: Three-Act Structure

source.originator: Aristotle (Poetics); formalized for screenwriting by Syd Field
source.work: Poetics (c. 335 BCE); Screenplay: The Foundations of Screenwriting (1979)
source.note: Field divided a screenplay into Setup / Confrontation / Resolution, roughly 25% / 50% / 25% of runtime, separated by two Plot Points.

definition: A story divides into a Setup (introduces protagonist, world, and dramatic premise), a Confrontation (protagonist pursues a goal against escalating obstacles), and a Resolution (the goal is won, lost, or transformed, and the story's tensions resolve). Two Plot Points mark the transitions: Plot Point 1 (~20-27% mark) ends Act One by radically redirecting the protagonist into Act Two's central conflict; Plot Point 2 (~75-80% mark) ends Act Two, usually at a low point, launching the final confrontation.
detection_signal: Identify which scene functions as Plot Point 1 (the scene after which the protagonist's central pursuit becomes irreversible) and Plot Point 2 (the scene that triggers the final act's confrontation/resolution sequence). Check their position against the expected page/scene-percentage range.
counter_considerations: Ensemble pieces, anthology structures, and some literary/arthouse scripts deliberately subvert or omit clean act breaks. Field himself stressed page numbers are guides, not requirements — flag deviation as a discussion point, not an error.

name: Save the Cat 15-Beat Sheet

source.work: Save the Cat! The Last Book on Screenwriting You'll Ever Need (2005)
source.note: Percentages below are Snyder's target placements for a standard ~110-page screenplay; treated as proportional guides, not fixed rules.

definition: A 15-beat elaboration of the three-act structure, designed to keep the large, easy-to-sag second act on track. In order: Opening Image (0-1%) sets tone via a 'before' snapshot; Theme Stated (~5%) has a supporting character voice the story's thematic question; Setup (1-10%) establishes the hero's flawed status quo; Catalyst (~10%) is the inciting event; Debate (10-20%) shows the hero hesitating before committing; Break into Two (20%) is the hero's active choice to enter the new world/plan; B Story (~22%) introduces a secondary relationship that carries the theme; Fun and Games (20-50%) delivers on the story's core premise/promise; Midpoint (50%) raises stakes via a false victory or false defeat; Bad Guys Close In (50-75%) escalates both external and internal pressure; All Is Lost (75%) is the hero's lowest point, often marked by a 'whiff of death'; Dark Night of the Soul (75-80%) is the hero's despair before finding new resolve; Break into Three (80%) is the hero's renewed plan combining lessons from A and B stories; Finale (80-99%) executes the final confrontation; Final Image (99-100%) mirrors the Opening Image to show transformation.
detection_signal: For each beat, identify the scene(s) that most plausibly fulfill its narrative function, and compare its position (as a percentage of total scene count or page count) against the target range. Flag beats that are missing entirely, or land far outside their expected range without clear narrative justification.
counter_considerations: This is one structural lens among several (compare Syd Field's simpler two-plot-point paradigm, Vogler's Hero's Journey) — a script that doesn't match Save the Cat's specific rhythm isn't necessarily broken, especially outside mainstream genre filmmaking. Snyder's percentages assume a ~110-page feature; adjust proportionally for shorts, pilots, or unusually long scripts.

name: Hero's Journey (12 Stages)

source.work: The Writer's Journey: Mythic Structure for Writers (1992/2007); adapted from Campbell's The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949)
source.note: Vogler condensed Campbell's more elaborate mythological stages into 12 practical screenwriting stages, grouped into three phases: Departure, Initiation, Return.

definition: Ordinary World (protagonist's status quo, hinting at what's missing); Call to Adventure (a problem or opportunity disrupts the status quo); Refusal of the Call (hesitation, fear, or reluctance); Meeting the Mentor (guidance or a tool is provided); Crossing the Threshold (commitment to the new world/journey, no return to the old status quo); Tests, Allies, Enemies (the protagonist learns the new world's rules through smaller conflicts); Approach to the Inmost Cave (preparation before the central ordeal); The Ordeal (a life-or-death crisis, the central crisis of the story); Reward/Seizing the Sword (the protagonist claims what they sought, but the story isn't over); The Road Back (recommitment to finishing the journey, often with new complications); Resurrection (a final, climactic test that proves the protagonist's transformation is real); Return with the Elixir (the protagonist returns changed, bringing benefit to their world).
detection_signal: Identify which scene(s) fulfill each of the 12 stages. Particularly check that Crossing the Threshold represents a genuine point of no return (not merely a change of location), and that Resurrection is a distinct, climactic test separate from The Ordeal.
counter_considerations: This is a mythological/archetypal lens best suited to journey- and transformation-driven stories (action, fantasy, adventure, many dramas). It fits less naturally onto ensemble pieces, procedurals, or stories without a single clear protagonist — don't force-fit it onto scripts where it doesn't apply.

name: Five-Part Story Design

source.work: Story: Substance, Structure, Style, and the Principles of Screenwriting (1997)

definition: A story's macro-structure runs: Inciting Incident (a disruptive event launches the protagonist toward an Object of Desire) -> Progressive Complications (escalating antagonism forces harder and harder choices, each crossing a point of no return) -> Crisis (the protagonist faces a true dilemma between two significant, irreconcilable goods, or the lesser of two evils, on the way to the climax) -> Climax (the final action that resolves the story's central question) -> Resolution (loose ends, if any, are tied off after the climax).
detection_signal: Verify progressive complications actually escalate in stakes/difficulty rather than repeating similar-magnitude obstacles, and confirm the Crisis presents a genuine dilemma (not an obvious choice) immediately before the Climax.
counter_considerations: Some scripts (especially slice-of-life, ensemble, or literary work) deliberately resist a single unifying crisis/climax — treat absence as worth flagging for discussion, not as an automatic defect.

name: Escalation of Conflict (Law of Conflict)

source.work: Story: Substance, Structure, Style, and the Principles of Screenwriting (1997)
source.note: McKee's 'Law of Conflict': nothing moves a story forward except through conflict.

definition: Conflict and stakes should escalate across the story rather than plateau or repeat at the same intensity. Each complication should be harder to overcome than the last, forcing the protagonist to use more of themselves (skill, will, resources, moral compromise) as the story progresses.
detection_signal: Track the apparent stakes/difficulty of major obstacles scene-by-scene or act-by-act. Flag a sustained middle section where conflicts feel same-magnitude rather than escalating (this often manifests as the commonly-cited 'sagging second act').
counter_considerations: Escalation doesn't have to be constant/linear — a deliberate lull before a final escalation (the 'calm before the storm') is a legitimate rhythm device, not automatically a pacing failure.

name: Opening/Closing Image Bookend

source.work: Save the Cat! The Last Book on Screenwriting You'll Ever Need (2005)

definition: The story's opening and closing images/scenes are designed as a matched 'before and after' pair — visually or thematically echoing each other, but with the difference between them making the protagonist's transformation legible without dialogue explaining it.
detection_signal: Compare the opening scene and closing scene/image: is there a deliberate echo (setting, framing, an object, a line of dialogue mirrored and inverted) that makes the change visible?
counter_considerations: Not every genre or story needs an explicit visual bookend — this is most load-bearing in visually-driven, transformation-centered narratives; less relevant for ensemble or plot-driven procedurals.
